questions.question: May ordained Cathari who come over to the Catholic and Apostolic Church remain in the clergy if they profess in writing to follow Catholic dogmas, including communion with the twice-married and with penitents who lapsed in persecution?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, if they come over to the Catholic and Apostolic Church, the great and holy Synod decrees that they who are ordained shall continue as.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That disciplinary or dogmatic settlement is not accepted as binding on this communion’s terms.

questions.question: Must Melitian clergy be received only under the Alexandrian settlement that strips Meletius of authority and places succession under the bishop of Alexandria’s ratification?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Melitian clergy may be received under the synod’s terms, but Meletius himself is granted no authority or privilege; succession among those received requires the people’s election and the bishop of Alexandria’s concurrence.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The parallel hierarchy and Meletius’s claims are not extinguished under that Alexandrian settlement; the schism’s episcopal legitimacy is not surrendered on those terms.
questions.canonical_citation: Nicaea I Synodal Letter to the Church of Alexandria

questions.question: Is the Son of God true God from true God, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Son is true God from true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Son is not of one substance with the Father. He is a created being—or otherwise not true God in the same sense as the Father—and is subordinate to him.

groups.group_name: Church of the East (Assyrian Church of the East)

questions.question: Must the letter said to be of Ibas to Maris—denying that the Word was made man of Mary Mother of God and attacking Cyril and Ephesus—be rejected rather than defended?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. That letter is to be rejected, not defended; its denial of the Word made man of Mary Mother of God and its attack on Cyril and Ephesus are condemned.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That letter’s sharper distinction of divinity and humanity may be defended; the Cyrilline anathematizing settlement is not accepted as binding in that way.

questions.question: Is the ever-virgin Mary exactly and truly the Mother of God, because God the Word was made flesh and born of her?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. She is exactly and truly the Mother of God, because God the Word begotten of the Father was in these last days made flesh and born of her.
questions.breakaway_answer: No—not as that forced ‘exactly and truly’ Theotokos confession. Mother of Christ language is preferred, keeping divinity and humanity distinct.

questions.question: Is the Emmanuel very God, and is the Holy Virgin therefore Mother of God (Theotokos) because she bore the Word of God made flesh?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Emmanuel is very God, and the Holy Virgin is Mother of God inasmuch as she bore the Word made flesh.
questions.breakaway_answer: No—not under that forced Theotokos settlement. She is confessed as Mother of Christ; divinity and humanity remain sharply distinguished as two qnome.

questions.question: Is our Great High Priest the divine Word made flesh himself, or another man distinct from the Word?
questions.catholic_answer: The divine Word made flesh himself is our Great High Priest and Apostle. There is not another man, distinct from the Word, who offers sacrifice for us.
questions.breakaway_answer: Not as a forced identity of the high priest with the Word alone. The high-priestly work is confessed in the humanity as distinct from the divinity (two qnome), without collapsing them into one subject in that way.

questions.question: Does the flesh of the Lord give life because it is the Word’s own flesh?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Lord’s flesh gives life because it is the Word’s own flesh, belonging to him as his very own.
questions.breakaway_answer: No—not under that forced wording. The flesh may be life-giving, yet divinity and humanity remain sharply distinct qnome rather than one flesh that is simply ‘the Word’s own’ in that sense.

questions.question: Did the Word of God suffer, get crucified, and taste death in the flesh?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Word of God suffered, was crucified, and tasted death in the flesh—those passions are truly said of the Word in his flesh.
questions.breakaway_answer: No—not in that sense. The Word’s divinity remains impassible; suffering, crucifixion, and death belong to the humanity distinctly, not to the divine nature.

questions.question: After the hypostatic union, may one divide the hypostases in the one Christ as joined only by worthiness or authority rather than by natural union?
questions.catholic_answer: No. After the hypostatic union one may not divide the hypostases as joined only by worthiness or authority. The union is a real, natural coming-together in one Christ.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes, in this sense: divinity and humanity remain two qnome sharply distinguished. Their connection is not that ‘natural union’ which would erase the dual integrity of the natures.

questions.question: May scriptural sayings about Christ be divided between two persons—some to a man apart from the Word, others only to the Word as God?
questions.catholic_answer: No. Scriptural sayings about Christ must not be split between two persons—some applied only to a man apart from the Word, others only to the Word as God. They are said of the one Christ.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes, in a careful dyophysite assignment: some sayings belong to the humanity, others to the divinity, because the two qnome are not collapsed into one subject of attribution.

questions.question: Is the assumed man to be worshipped together with the Word as two different things, or is Emmanuel worshipped with one adoration?
questions.catholic_answer: Emmanuel is worshipped with one adoration. The assumed man is not worshipped together with the Word as two different things side by side.
questions.breakaway_answer: Worship may honor the distinction of the two qnome. A single ‘one adoration’ that forbids any dual reference is not required; the humanity is not absorbed into an undifferentiated cult of the Word alone.

questions.question: Was the one Lord Jesus Christ glorified by the Holy Spirit as using a power not his own, or as his own Spirit working miracles?
questions.catholic_answer: He was glorified by his own Spirit working miracles—not by using a power foreign to himself.
questions.breakaway_answer: Not under that forced alternative. The Spirit’s wonders in Christ are confessed while keeping the distinction of divinity and humanity, without accepting that exclusive wording.

questions.question: If bishops subscribe Nestorius’s deposition and then reverse course, are they to be treated as having joined apostasy from Ephesus’s judgment?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Bishops who reverse after subscribing that deposition have joined apostasy and are to be removed from the priesthood; the deposition stands as binding orthodoxy.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That deposition is not binding orthodoxy. Communion may continue without treating reversal of subscription as apostasy from the faith.

questions.question: Is it unlawful to compose or introduce a creed different from the faith of Nicaea as received by the Council of Ephesus?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. It is unlawful to compose or introduce a creed different from the faith already established by the fathers in the Holy Spirit; that creed alone settles the faith for reception.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That ban is not authoritative. The faith may be confessed in a different settlement that distinguishes divinity and humanity more sharply than that synod required.

questions.question: Is the Holy Virgin rightly called Mother of God (Theotokos) because the Word united to flesh is one Christ and one Son from two natures in true union?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Virgin is rightly called Mother of God, because the Word united to flesh is one Christ and one Son from two natures in true union—not because the Godhead began from her.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The preferred title is Mother of Christ. Mother of God is not required; it risks confusing the natures if taken as that settlement enforced it.
questions.canonical_citation: Ephesus, Epistle of Cyril to Nestorius (Intelligo quosdam)

questions.question: Must the Constantinopolitan creed be sung with the Filioque, and must Chalcedon’s two natures and the sixth council’s two wills be accepted?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The creed is to be received with ‘and the Son,’ and Chalcedon’s two natures in one person and the sixth council’s two wills are to be accepted.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Filioque addition is refused, and Christ is confessed in the miaphysite settlement rather than under those two-natures and two-wills union terms.

questions.question: Did Chalcedon and Pope Leo rightly define the truth about two natures in Christ?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. That synod and that pope rightly defined the truth about two natures in the one person of Christ.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. They did not rightly define that truth. After the union there is one united nature of the Word incarnate, not two natures as they taught.

questions.question: In the sacrifice of the altar, must a little water be mixed with the wine in the chalice?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. While the chalice is offered, a little water is to be mixed with the wine.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The wine is offered unmixed; mixing water with the wine at the altar is not required.

questions.question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, are the penitent cleansed after death by purifying pains, and does the Roman pontiff hold primacy over the whole Church?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; the penitent may be cleansed after death by purifying pains; and the Roman pontiff holds primacy over the whole Church.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Spirit proceeds from the Father; that purgatory formulation of purifying pains is not received; and Roman universal primacy is refused.

questions.question: Must the Constantinopolitan creed be received with the added phrase 'and the Son' (Filioque) and used in the Armenian churches as Florence decrees?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The creed must be received with the added phrase ‘and the Son,’ as a licit clarification of the truth, and used in the liturgy as decreed.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The creed must stand without that added phrase. Requiring ‘and the Son’ as a condition of communion is rejected; procession is confessed from the Father.

questions.question: Must the Armenians (and those entering Latin union) accept Chalcedon’s definition of two natures in the one person of Christ?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Those entering union must accept the definition of two natures in the one person of Christ as the faith of the universal synods.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That two-nature definition is not the price of communion. The faith is the miaphysite confession of one united nature of the Word incarnate.

questions.question: Must the Armenians accept Chalcedon and Pope Leo, contrary to the claim that both taught Nestorius’s heresy?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. They must accept that later synod and that pope. The claim that both taught the condemned dyophysite heresy is false; their definition is orthodox.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. They are not to be accepted on those terms. The charge that they teach heresy is not settled by submitting to them; the miaphysite confession stands without that acceptance.

questions.question: Can anyone outside the Catholic Church—pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics—share eternal life unless joined to that Church before death?
questions.catholic_answer: No. Those outside the Church—pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics—cannot share eternal life unless joined to it before death. Only those who abide in that unity share the Church’s sacraments unto salvation.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes, eternal life is not closed to everyone outside that Latin communion. Salvation is found in the older Eastern church of the fathers; joining that Roman-defined body is not the condition of eternal life.

questions.question: Should the second synod of Ephesus be condemned as impious for approving Eutychian error under Dioscorus?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. That second synod should be condemned as impious for approving Eutychian error under its Alexandrian president, who defended that heresy and persecuted the orthodox bishop of Constantinople.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That synod and its president are not to be condemned as impious Eutychian partisans. The president is remembered as a defender of orthodoxy against a wrong settlement, not as a heresiarch’s champion.

questions.question: Must Christians embrace the Council of Chalcedon (630 fathers) as a universal council of the Church?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Christians must embrace that council of the 630 fathers as a universal council of the Church, fourth among the ecumenical synods.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. It is not a universal council of the Church. The binding christological settlement is the earlier miaphysite confession, not that two-nature definition.

questions.question: Must Christians accept Constantinople II, which renewed Chalcedon’s definition of two natures in one person of Christ?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Christians must accept that fifth synod, including its renewal of the two-nature definition in one person of Christ and its condemnation of Origenist errors.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That synod is not accepted insofar as it renews the two-nature definition as binding. Orthodoxy is confessed in the miaphysite tradition without that renewal.

questions.question: Must Christians accept Constantinople III’s definition that in Christ there are two natures, two principles of action, and two wills in one person?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. In Christ there are two perfect natures, two principles of action, and two wills, in one and the same person.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That dyothelete / two-natures package is not required for communion. Christ is confessed in the miaphysite tradition without accepting those dualities as the binding settlement.

questions.question: Are universal synods those legitimately confirmed by the authority of a Roman pontiff, including Florence’s unions with the Greeks and Armenians?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Universal synods are those legitimately confirmed by the Roman pontiff’s authority, including the recent unions and their definitions.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Universal synods are not defined by papal confirmation. Authority rests in the consensus of the ancient churches; those unions are not binding conditions of the faith.

questions.question: May fourth and further marriages be lawfully contracted when no canonical impediment exists?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. When no canonical impediment exists, not only second and third but also fourth and further marriages may lawfully be contracted.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Repeated remarriage is restricted; fourth and further marriages are not treated as freely lawful in that way.

questions.question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, as the holy Roman church professes in its teaching on the Trinity?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: one God in three persons, the Spirit having his being from both.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. Procession ‘from the Father and the Son’ as from one principle is not confessed.

questions.question: Is one and the same Son perfect in divinity and humanity, true God and true man, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. One and the same Son is perfect in divinity and humanity, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. After the union he is confessed as one united nature of the Word incarnate, not ‘in two natures’ as that definition requires.

questions.question: Is Christ’s body truly confected in both unleavened and leavened bread, and are souls who die penitent but without full satisfaction cleansed after death by cleansing pains, aided by the Church’s suffrages?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes on both counts. Christ’s body is truly confected in either unleavened or leavened wheat bread according to each church’s rite; and penitent souls who die without full satisfaction are cleansed after death by cleansing pains, helped by the suffrages of the living.
questions.breakaway_answer: No on purgatorial cleansing pains and those Mass-centered suffrages as defined—the dead are prayed for, but not under that doctrine. Unleavened bread also remains contested; leavened bread is the proper use in the Eastern rite.

questions.question: Do souls free of sin (or cleansed of it) go straight to the beatific vision, while those dying in mortal or original sin alone go straight to hell?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Purified souls go straight to the beatific vision, graded by merits; those dying in mortal sin or original sin alone go straight to hell, with unequal pains.
questions.breakaway_answer: Not under that immediate heaven-or-hell schema as defined. The destiny of souls after death is confessed with prayer for the dead, without accepting that Latin mapping of destinies.

questions.question: Does the Roman pontiff rank first among the patriarchs, with Constantinople second, then Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Roman pontiff ranks first among the patriarchs, then Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, without prejudice to their privileges.
questions.breakaway_answer: No as a claim of supreme jurisdiction. A primacy of honor among equals may be granted to Rome; first place with power over the whole Church is rejected.

questions.question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle and a single spiration?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle and a single spiration, having his being from both.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone as cause. Eternal procession from Father and Son as from one principle is rejected.

questions.question: Because the Father gave the Son everything except being the Father, does the Son also have it from the Father that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Because the Father gave the Son everything except being the Father, the Son also eternally has it that the Spirit proceeds from the Son.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That inference does not hold. What the Son receives in being begotten does not include causing the Spirit’s procession; the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

questions.question: Was it licit to add the explanation 'and from the Son' (Filioque) to the Creed for the sake of declaring the truth?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Adding ‘and from the Son’ to the Creed was licit and reasonable, under urgent necessity, to declare the truth of the Spirit’s procession.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Creed must not be altered by that insertion. The faith is confessed with the older wording; adding the phrase was not licit.

questions.question: Is the Holy Spirit true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Holy Spirit is true God, coequal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son.
questions.breakaway_answer: The Holy Spirit is true God, coequal with the Father and the Son, but proceeds from the Father—not from the Father and the Son.
questions.canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 463)

questions.question: If the baptized die truly repentant before making full satisfaction, are their souls cleansed after death by purifying punishments, helped by Masses, prayers, and alms?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Such souls are cleansed after death by purifying punishments, and the offerings of the living—Masses, prayers, and alms—relieve those pains.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. There is no such state of purifying punishments after death relieved by Masses. The dead are commemorated and prayed for, but not under that purgatorial doctrine.
questions.canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 464)

questions.question: Does the Roman Church rightly teach seven sacraments and prepare the Eucharist from unleavened bread, with the bread changed into Christ’s body and the wine into his blood?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. There are seven sacraments, and the Eucharist is prepared from unleavened bread, the bread changed into Christ’s body and the wine into his blood.
questions.breakaway_answer: Seven mysteries may be honored in another sense, but unleavened bread is not the norm—leavened bread is used. That Latin sacramental package is not binding as a condition of faith.
questions.canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 465)

questions.question: Does the Roman Church hold the highest and complete primacy and spiritual power over the universal Catholic Church, received in Peter by the Roman pontiff?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The highest and complete primacy and spiritual power over the universal Church belongs to that see in Peter’s successor, received from the Lord with fullness of power.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That see does not hold universal supremacy. Primacy, if any, is honor among sister churches, not complete spiritual power over the whole Church.
questions.canonical_citation: Lyons II, Profession of Faith of Michael Palaeologus (Denzinger 466)

questions.question: Must everyone who raises a heresy against the Catholic faith as there explained be excommunicated and anathematized as a heretic under that regime?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Every heresy raised against that faith is excommunicated and anathematized; those condemned are handed over for due punishment, clerics being first degraded from their orders.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Lay preaching and apostolic poverty outside that episcopal license are not condemned heresy under that regime; the anathematizing of such dissenters is refused.

questions.question: After consecration, does the host remain true bread in nature while being Christ’s body only figuratively (remanence)?
questions.catholic_answer: No. After consecration the host does not remain true bread in substance. The whole substance is converted; Christ’s body is truly present, not only figuratively.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes. After consecration the host remains true bread in nature while being Christ’s body figuratively—or in figure—so remanence is affirmed.
questions.canonical_citation: Constance S15 [Articles of John Wyclif selected from the 260]

questions.question: Was John Wyclif rightly judged a heretic whose memory and teaching are to be condemned?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. He was rightly judged a heretic whose memory and teaching are to be condemned; the process found no lawful defender.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. He was not a heretic. His memory and teaching should be honored as gospel reform, not condemned.
questions.canonical_citation: Constance S8 [The council pronounces John Wyclif a heretic, condemns his memory and orders his bones to be exhumed]

questions.question: Must the Christian people receive the Eucharist under both bread and wine, so that the laity communicate under the wine as well?
questions.catholic_answer: No. The approved custom of communion under one kind for the laity stands; the people are not bound to receive under both kinds.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes. The sacrament should be given to the people under both kinds; withholding the cup from the laity is refused.
questions.canonical_citation: Constance S13 [Condemnation of communion under both kinds, recently revived among the Bohemians by Jakoubek of Stribro]

questions.question: Is the one holy universal church identical with the total number of those predestined to salvation?
questions.catholic_answer: No. The one holy universal church is not simply identical with the set of the predestined. The visible Church is the communion of the baptized under rightful pastors, not that number alone.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes. The one holy universal church is precisely the total number of those predestined to salvation—that is what ‘church’ means.
questions.canonical_citation: Constance S15 [Condemned articles of J. Hus]

questions.question: Was John Hus rightly condemned by Constance as a heretic for obstinately holding Wycliffite and related errors?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. He was rightly condemned as a heretic for obstinately holding those errors against the faith.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. He was not rightly condemned. The sentence was unjust; he is to be honored as a faithful witness, not a heretic.

questions.question: Was Jerome of Prague rightly condemned by Constance as a heretic?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. He was rightly condemned as a heretic for not abiding in the faith as judged in that inquiry.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. He was not rightly condemned. He is to be honored among the faithful reformers and martyrs, not as a heretic.
questions.canonical_citation: Constance S21 [Sentence condemning Jerome of Prague]

questions.question: Must the Christian people receive the Eucharist under both bread and wine, so that the laity communicate under the wine as well?
questions.catholic_answer: No. The approved custom of communion under one kind for the laity stands; the people are not bound to receive under both kinds.
questions.breakaway_answer: Yes. The sacrament should be given under both kinds; withholding the cup from the people is refused.
questions.canonical_citation: Constance S13 [Condemnation of communion under both kinds, recently revived among the Bohemians by Jakoubek of Stribro]

questions.question: In the Eucharist, is the whole substance of bread and wine converted into Christ’s body and blood, with only the appearances remaining (transubstantiation)?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The whole substance of bread and wine is converted into Christ’s body and blood; only the appearances remain—that conversion is rightly called transubstantiation.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. There is no such conversion of the whole substance. Christ is present spiritually or sacramentally, or the elements remain bread and wine while signifying or conveying his body and blood.
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: For the entire remission of sins in the sacrament of Penance, are contrition, confession, and satisfaction required as its three parts?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Contrition, confession, and satisfaction are required as the three parts—as it were the matter—of that sacrament for the entire remission of sins.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Remission is not tied to those three acts as mandatory matter. Forgiveness comes by repentance and faith, without requiring auricular confession and satisfaction in that juridical form.
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: Did Christ institute the Sacrifice of the Mass as a true sacrifice of his body and blood?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Christ instituted the Sacrifice of the Mass as a true sacrifice of his body and blood, a visible sacrifice representing and continuing the sacrifice of the cross.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Christ did not institute a propitiatory Mass-sacrifice. He instituted the Lord’s Supper as communion and remembrance of his once-for-all death, not a repeated sacrificial offering.
questions.canonical_citation: Trent S22 Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass ch. 1
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: Is the Sacrifice of the Mass truly propitiatory for both the living and the dead?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. In the Mass the same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner; the sacrifice is truly propitiatory for the living and the dead.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. The Mass is not a propitiatory sacrifice for the living and the dead. Christ’s sacrifice on the cross was once for all; the Supper does not re-offer him for sin.
questions.canonical_citation: Trent S22 Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass ch. 2
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: May Masses be offered in honor of the saints?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Masses may be offered in honor of the saints to obtain their intercession, while the sacrifice itself is offered to God alone.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Masses should not be offered in honor of the saints. Worship and sacrificial offering belong to God alone; the saints are not to be honored that way in the Supper.
questions.canonical_citation: Trent S22 Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass ch. 3
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: Is the Canon of the Mass free from error and rightly retained as the Church’s holy prayer for offering the sacrifice?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. The Canon of the Mass is free from error—drawn from the Lord’s words and apostolic piety—and is rightly retained for offering the sacrifice.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. That Canon is not free from error as a sacrificial prayer and should not be retained. The Supper should use a rite without that propitiatory canon.
questions.canonical_citation: Trent S22 Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass ch. 4
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: Has the Church rightly instituted solemn Mass ceremonies—lights, incense, vestments, and varied tones of voice—as helps to divine worship?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Lights, incense, vestments, and varied tones of voice are rightly instituted so that human minds may be raised to divine things.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Those ceremonies are not apostolic necessities. Ritual may be simplified or stripped; such externals are human tradition, not required helps to true worship.
questions.canonical_citation: Trent S22 Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass ch. 5
questions.notes: Umbrella label: concrete Protestant confessions vary; answer states the Reformational position Trent is targeting. Primary Trent interlocutor; Reformed/Anglican/Anabaptist often share the rejection.

questions.question: Are Masses in which the priest alone communicates sacramentally lawful and to be approved?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Masses in which the priest alone communicates are lawful and approved; they remain true sacrifices even when the faithful do not communicate sacramentally.
questions.breakaway_answer: No. Private Masses of that kind are not lawful. The Lord’s Supper is a communion of the faithful; a priest communicating alone is not the Supper Christ instituted.

questions.question: Has the Church erred in teaching that the marriage bond cannot be dissolved by adultery and that neither party may marry another during the other’s life?

questions.question: After baptism, are little children to be reckoned among the faithful even without actual faith of their own, so that omitting their baptism—or rebaptizing them later—is forbidden?
questions.catholic_answer: Yes. Little children after baptism are reckoned among the faithful; they are not to be rebaptized when they reach discretion, and it is not better to omit their baptism for lack of their own act of faith.
